title: Thermodynamics
subtitle: Zero-to-JEE-Advanced Visual Textbook: Zeroth & First Laws, Internal Energy, Work on P-V Indicator Diagrams, Isochoric/Isobaric/Isothermal/Adiabatic/Polytropic Processes, Cyclic Processes, Carnot Engine & Second Law
introduction:
💡 First-Time Reader Intuition: What Is Thermodynamics?

Thermodynamics literally means “Heat in Motion”—it is the branch of Physics that studies how thermal energy ($Q$) is converted into mechanical work ($W$) and vice versa. From steam locomotives and car engines to refrigerators and power plants, every heat machine in the modern world runs on the laws of this chapter.

System, Surroundings & State vs. Path Functions:
  • Thermodynamic System: A specific macroscopic collection of matter (typically $n$ moles of an ideal gas inside a cylinder fitted with a movable piston) that we choose to study. Everything outside it is the Surroundings.
  • State Functions (Point Functions — $P, V, T, U, S$): Quantities whose change depends ONLY on the initial and final equilibrium states, completely independent of the path taken! In any closed cycle, $\Delta U = 0, \Delta T = 0, \Delta P = 0$.
  • Path Functions ($Q$ and $W$): Heat supplied ($Q$) and Work done ($W$) are NOT state functions! They depend entirely on the specific path taken on a $P$-$V$ diagram.

topics.title: Zeroth Law, Internal Energy, P-V Indicator Work & First Law of Thermodynamics
topics.theoryHtml:
1.1 Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics & Internal Energy ($U$)
Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics:
If system $A$ is in thermal equilibrium with system $C$, and system $B$ is also separately in thermal equilibrium with system $C$, then $A$ and $B$ are in thermal equilibrium with each other ($T_A = T_B = T_C$). This law defines the physical concept of Temperature.

Internal Energy ($U$) of an Ideal Gas:
In an ideal gas, there are no intermolecular attractions ($U_{\text{potential}} = 0$). Therefore, internal energy is purely the sum of the random thermal kinetic energies of all gas molecules, which depends ONLY on absolute temperature $T$ and degrees of freedom $f$:

$$\boxed{U = \frac{f}{2}n R T = n C_V T} \implies \boxed{\Delta U = n C_V \Delta T = \frac{f}{2}n R \Delta T = \frac{f}{2}(P_f V_f - P_i V_i)}$$

Crucial JEE Rule: The formula $\Delta U = n C_V \Delta T$ is universally true for EVERY process of an ideal gas (whether isochoric, isobaric, isothermal, adiabatic, or arbitrary), because $U$ is a state function!

1.2 Mechanical Work Done by a Gas ($W$) & First Law of Thermodynamics

When a gas at pressure $P$ pushes a piston of area $A$ outward by a tiny distance $dx$, the volume increases by $dV = A\,dx$, and the work done BY the gas is $dW = F\,dx = (PA)dx = P\,dV$:

$$\boxed{W_{\text{by gas}} = \int_{V_i}^{V_f} P\,dV = \text{Area under } P\text{-}V \text{ curve projected onto the Volume axis}}$$
First Law of Thermodynamics (Conservation of Energy):
When heat $Q$ is supplied to a system, part of it goes into changing the internal energy ($\Delta U$) and the rest is used by the system to do external work ($W$):
$$\boxed{Q = \Delta U + W} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{Differential Form:} \quad \boxed{dQ = dU + dW = n C_V\,dT + P\,dV}$$
QuantityPositive ($+$) Sign (Physics Convention)Negative ($-$) Sign (Physics Convention)
Heat ($Q$)Heat absorbed by (added to) the gas.Heat rejected by (taken out of) the gas.
Work ($W$)Gas expands ($V_f > V_i$, work done BY gas).Gas is compressed ($V_f < V_i$, work done ON gas).
Internal Energy ($\Delta U$)Temperature rises ($T_f > T_i$).Temperature falls ($T_f < T_i$).
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation of Mayer's Relation: C_P − C_V = R

Consider $n$ moles of an ideal gas heated by $dT$ at constant pressure (Isobaric process):

Step 1: Heat supplied at constant pressure is $dQ_P = n C_P\,dT$, and internal energy change is $dU = n C_V\,dT$.

Step 2: From the Ideal Gas Law $PV = nRT$, differentiating at constant pressure $P$ gives $P\,dV = nR\,dT$, so work done is $dW = P\,dV = nR\,dT$.

Step 3: Substitute into the First Law $dQ_P = dU + dW$:

$$n C_P\,dT = n C_V\,dT + n R\,dT \implies \boxed{C_P - C_V = R}$$

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Physics vs. Chemistry Sign of Work $W$): In Physics, $W = +\int P\,dV$ is work done BY the gas, so $Q = \Delta U + W$ (expansion is $+W$). In Chemistry, $W_{\text{chem}} = -\int P\,dV$ is work done ON the gas, so $\Delta U = Q + W_{\text{chem}}$. In JEE Physics, ALWAYS use $Q = \Delta U + W_{\text{by gas}}$!
  • Trap 2 (Projecting Area onto the WRONG Axis): Work $W = \int P\,dV$ is ALWAYS the area projected onto the Volume ($V$) axis, even if the question plots $V$ on the vertical axis and $P$ on the horizontal axis!

topics.title: Standard Processes I: Isochoric, Isobaric & Isothermal Processes and Specific Heats of Gases
topics.theoryHtml:

topics.derivationHtml:
Calculus Derivation of Isothermal Work Done & Isothermal Bulk Modulus

1. Isothermal Work ($T = \text{constant}$): Substitute $P = \frac{nRT}{V}$ into $W = \int_{V_i}^{V_f} P\,dV$:

$$W = nRT \int_{V_i}^{V_f} \frac{dV}{V} = \boxed{nRT \ln\left(\frac{V_f}{V_i}\right) = 2.3026\,nRT \log_{10}\left(\frac{V_f}{V_i}\right)}$$

2. Isothermal Slope & Bulk Modulus ($B_T$): Differentiating $PV = \text{constant}$ gives $P\,dV + V\,dP = 0$:

$$\text{Slope of Isotherm on } P\text{-}V \text{ graph:} \quad \boxed{\left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_T = -\frac{P}{V}} \implies \boxed{B_T = -V\frac{dP}{dV} = P}$$

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Isobaric Fraction of Heat Converted to Work vs. Internal Energy): In ANY isobaric expansion, the fraction of supplied heat that goes into increasing internal energy is $\frac{\Delta U}{Q_P} = \frac{n C_V \Delta T}{n C_P \Delta T} = \mathbf{\frac{1}{\gamma}}$, and the fraction converted into work is $\frac{W}{Q_P} = \mathbf{1 - \frac{1}{\gamma}}$! For a diatomic gas ($\gamma = 7/5 = 1.4$), $\frac{\Delta U}{Q_P} = \frac{5}{7}$ and $\frac{W}{Q_P} = \frac{2}{7}$.

topics.title: Standard Processes II: Adiabatic Process, Polytropic Process & Free Expansion in Vacuum
topics.theoryHtml:
3.1 Adiabatic Process ($Q = 0$, Rapid or Thermally Insulated Process)
Definition:
A process in which no heat enters or leaves the system ($Q = 0$), either because the cylinder walls are thermally insulated or because the process happens extremely fast (like a tire bursting or sound waves propagating in air). By First Law: $0 = \Delta U + W \implies \boxed{W = -\Delta U}$!
$$\textbf{Poisson's 3 Adiabatic Equations:} \qquad \boxed{P V^\gamma = \text{const}} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \boxed{T V^{\gamma - 1} = \text{const}} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \boxed{P^{1 - \gamma} T^\gamma = \text{const}}$$
$$\textbf{Work Done in Adiabatic Process:} \qquad \boxed{W_{\text{adia}} = -\Delta U = \frac{n R (T_i - T_f)}{\gamma - 1} = \frac{P_i V_i - P_f V_f}{\gamma - 1}}$$

Slope & Bulk Modulus of an Adiabatic Curve vs. Isothermal Curve:
Differentiating $PV^\gamma = \text{const}$ gives $V^\gamma dP + \gamma P V^{\gamma - 1}dV = 0$:

$$\boxed{\left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_{\text{adia}} = -\gamma\left(\frac{P}{V}\right) = \gamma \times \left(\frac{dP}{dV}\right)_{\text{iso}}} \implies \boxed{B_{\text{adia}} = \gamma P}$$

Since $\gamma > 1$, an adiabatic curve is ALWAYS steeper than an isothermal curve passing through the same point by a factor of $\gamma$!

3.2 Polytropic Process ($PV^x = \text{Constant}$) & Free Expansion
$$\textbf{Polytropic Process } (PV^x = \text{const}): \quad \boxed{W = \frac{P_i V_i - P_f V_f}{x - 1} = \frac{nR(T_i - T_f)}{x - 1}} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \textbf{Molar Heat Capacity:} \quad \boxed{C = C_V + \frac{R}{1 - x}}$$
Free Expansion of an Ideal Gas into Vacuum (Joule Expansion):
If an insulated vessel is divided by a partition with gas in one half and vacuum ($P_{\text{ext}} = 0$) in the other, and the partition suddenly ruptures:
  • External resisting pressure is zero, so $\mathbf{W = 0}$.
  • Walls are insulated, so $\mathbf{Q = 0}$.
  • By First Law, $\mathbf{\Delta U = 0 \implies \Delta T = 0 \implies T_f = T_i}$ (and $P_f V_f = P_i V_i$)!
topics.derivationHtml:
Calculus Proof of PV^γ = Constant & Polytropic Heat Capacity C = C_V + R/(1 − x)

1. Proof of $PV^\gamma = \text{constant}$: In an adiabatic process, $dQ = nC_V\,dT + P\,dV = 0$. Substitute $dT = \frac{P\,dV + V\,dP}{nR}$ and $R = C_P - C_V$:

$$C_V(P\,dV + V\,dP) + (C_P - C_V)P\,dV = 0 \implies C_V V\,dP + C_P P\,dV = 0$$

Divide by $C_V P V$ and use $\gamma = C_P/C_V$:

$$\frac{dP}{P} + \gamma\frac{dV}{V} = 0 \implies \ln P + \gamma \ln V = \text{const} \implies \boxed{P V^\gamma = \text{Constant}}$$

2. Polytropic Molar Heat Capacity ($PV^x = \text{const}$): Since $dQ = dU + dW = nC_V\,dT + \frac{nR\,dT}{1 - x}$, dividing by $n\,dT$ gives $\boxed{C = \frac{dQ}{n\,dT} = C_V + \frac{R}{1 - x}}$.

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Isothermal vs. Adiabatic Curve Position in Expansion vs. Compression): Because the adiabatic curve is steeper:
    • During Expansion ($V_1 \to V_2$), the Isothermal curve lies ABOVE the Adiabatic curve ($W_{\text{iso}} > W_{\text{adia}}$ and $P_{\text{iso}} > P_{\text{adia}}$).
    • During Compression ($V_1 \to V_2$), the Adiabatic curve rises ABOVE the Isothermal curve ($|W_{\text{adia}}| > |W_{\text{iso}}|$ and $P_{\text{adia}} > P_{\text{iso}}$)!
  • Trap 2 (Never Apply $PV^\gamma = \text{const}$ to Free Expansion!): Even though $Q = 0$ in free expansion into vacuum, free expansion is an irreversible non-quasi-static process, so $PV^\gamma = \text{const}$ is completely invalid! Instead, $\Delta T = 0$, so the initial and final states obey $P_i V_i = P_f V_f$.

topics.title: Cyclic Processes, Thermal Efficiency, Carnot Engine, Refrigerator COP & Second Law of Thermodynamics
topics.theoryHtml:
4.1 Cyclic Processes & Thermal Efficiency ($\eta$)
Cyclic Process Rule:
When a gas undergoes a complete cycle and returns to its exact initial state $(P_i, V_i, T_i)$, its net change in internal energy is strictly zero ($\Delta U_{\text{cycle}} = 0$). Therefore, net heat absorbed equals the area enclosed by the loop:
$$\boxed{\Delta U_{\text{cycle}} = 0 \implies Q_{\text{net}} = W_{\text{net}} = \oint P\,dV = \text{Area Enclosed by Loop}}$$
  • Clockwise Loop (with $P$ on y-axis, $V$ on x-axis): Expansion happens at higher pressure than compression $\implies \mathbf{W_{\text{net}} > 0}$ (Acts as a Heat Engine).
  • Counter-Clockwise (Anticlockwise) Loop: Compression happens at higher pressure than expansion $\implies \mathbf{W_{\text{net}} < 0}$ (Acts as a Refrigerator / Heat Pump).
$$\textbf{Efficiency of Any Thermodynamic Cycle:} \qquad \boxed{\eta = \frac{\text{Net Work Done } (W_{\text{net}})}{\text{Total POSITIVE Heat Absorbed } (Q_{\text{in}})} = 1 - \frac{|Q_{\text{out}}|}{Q_{\text{in}}}}$$
4.2 Carnot Engine, Refrigerator COP & Second Law of Thermodynamics
$$\textbf{1. Carnot Reversible Engine Efficiency:} \qquad \boxed{\eta_{\text{Carnot}} = 1 - \frac{Q_C}{Q_H} = 1 - \frac{T_C}{T_H}} \quad (T_C, T_H \text{ strictly in Kelvin!})$$
$$\textbf{2. Refrigerator Coefficient of Performance (COP):} \qquad \boxed{\beta = \frac{\text{Heat Extracted from Cold Box } (Q_C)}{\text{Work Input } (W)} = \frac{Q_C}{Q_H - Q_C} = \frac{T_C}{T_H - T_C}} = \frac{1 - \eta}{\eta}$$
Second Law of Thermodynamics:
• Kelvin-Planck Statement: It is impossible to construct a cyclic heat engine that absorbs heat from a single reservoir and converts $100\%$ of it into work without rejecting some heat to a colder sink ($\eta < 100\%$).
• Clausius Statement: Heat cannot flow spontaneously from a colder body to a hotter body without external work being done on the system.
topics.derivationHtml:
Proof of Carnot Efficiency η = 1 − T_C / T_H

A Carnot cycle consists of 4 reversible steps: (1) Isothermal expansion at $T_H$ ($V_1 \to V_2$, absorbs $Q_H = nRT_H\ln(V_2/V_1)$), (2) Adiabatic expansion ($V_2 \to V_3$, cools $T_H \to T_C$), (3) Isothermal compression at $T_C$ ($V_3 \to V_4$, rejects $|Q_C| = nRT_C\ln(V_3/V_4)$), and (4) Adiabatic compression ($V_4 \to V_1$, warms $T_C \to T_H$).

From the two adiabatic steps: $T_H V_2^{\gamma-1} = T_C V_3^{\gamma-1}$ and $T_H V_1^{\gamma-1} = T_C V_4^{\gamma-1}$. Dividing these two equations gives $\frac{V_2}{V_1} = \frac{V_3}{V_4}$! Therefore:

$$\frac{|Q_C|}{Q_H} = \frac{nRT_C\ln(V_3/V_4)}{nRT_H\ln(V_2/V_1)} = \frac{T_C}{T_H} \implies \boxed{\eta = 1 - \frac{|Q_C|}{Q_H} = 1 - \frac{T_C}{T_H}}$$

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Denominator of Cycle Efficiency $\eta = W_{\text{net}} / Q_{\text{in}}$): In the denominator $Q_{\text{in}}$, you must sum ONLY the steps where heat is positive ($Q > 0$, heat absorbed)! Never put $Q_{\text{net}}$ in the denominator (if you put $Q_{\text{net}}$ in the denominator, since $W_{\text{net}} = Q_{\text{net}}$, you would get $\eta = 100\%$ every time!).
  • Trap 2 (Lowering Sink Temperature $T_C$ vs. Raising Source Temperature $T_H$ by the Same $\Delta T$): Since $\eta_1 = 1 - \frac{T_C - \Delta T}{T_H} = 1 - \frac{T_C}{T_H} + \frac{\Delta T}{T_H}$ and $\eta_2 = 1 - \frac{T_C}{T_H + \Delta T}$, lowering the sink temperature $T_C$ by $\Delta T$ ALWAYS increases Carnot efficiency more than raising the source temperature $T_H$ by the same $\Delta T$!

conclusion: You have mastered Chapter 11: Thermodynamics! You can now analyze any gas process, indicator diagram, polytropic law, cyclic heat engine, or Carnot refrigerator from first principles.
summary:
• First Law: $Q = \Delta U + W$ where $\Delta U = nC_V\Delta T = \frac{f}{2}nR\Delta T$ (always) and $W = \int P\,dV$.
  • Mayer's Relation: $C_P - C_V = R$ and $\gamma = \frac{C_P}{C_V} = 1 + \frac{2}{f}$.
  • Work Formulas: Isochoric $W = 0$; Isobaric $W = P\Delta V = nR\Delta T$; Isothermal $W = nRT\ln(V_f/V_i)$; Adiabatic $W = \frac{P_i V_i - P_f V_f}{\gamma - 1}$.
  • Polytropic ($PV^x = \text{const}$): $C = C_V + \frac{R}{1-x}$.
  • Carnot Engine & Refrigerator: $\eta = 1 - \frac{T_C}{T_H}$ and $\text{COP} = \frac{T_C}{T_H - T_C}$.

Adiabatic ($Q = 0$)$PV^\gamma = \text{const}$$\dfrac{P_i V_i - P_f V_f}{\gamma - 1}$$W = -\Delta U, \; B_S = \gamma P$
Polytropic$PV^x = \text{const}$$\dfrac{nR(T_i - T_f)}{x - 1}$$C = C_V + \dfrac{R}{1 - x}$

questions.prompt: A gas absorbs $500\text{ J}$ of heat and performs $200\text{ J}$ of external work while expanding. What is the change in the internal energy $\Delta U$ of the gas?
questions.explanation: By the First Law of Thermodynamics, $Q = \Delta U + W \implies 500 = \Delta U + 200 \implies \Delta U = +300\text{ J}$.

questions.prompt: When a diatomic ideal gas ($\gamma = 1.4$) expands at constant pressure (isobaric process) by absorbing $700\text{ J}$ of heat, how much work is done by the gas?
questions.explanation: In an isobaric process, the fraction of heat converted into work is $\frac{W}{Q_P} = 1 - \frac{1}{\gamma} = 1 - \frac{5}{7} = \frac{2}{7}$. Thus $W = \frac{2}{7}(700\text{ J}) = 200\text{ J}$ (and $\Delta U = 500\text{ J}$).

questions.prompt: A Carnot heat engine operates between a hot source at $127^\circ\text{C}$ and a cold sink at $27^\circ\text{C}$. What is its thermal efficiency $\eta$?
questions.explanation: Convert temperatures to Kelvin first! $T_H = 127 + 273 = 400\text{ K}$ and $T_C = 27 + 273 = 300\text{ K}$. Therefore, $\eta = 1 - \frac{T_C}{T_H} = 1 - \frac{300}{400} = 0.25 = 25\%$.

questions.prompt: An ideal monoatomic gas ($\gamma = 5/3$) initially at $27^\circ\text{C}$ is suddenly compressed adiabatically to $\frac{8}{27}$ of its original volume. What will be the rise in temperature of the gas?
questions.explanation: Initial temperature $T_1 = 27 + 273 = 300\text{ K}$. Using $T_1 V_1^{\gamma - 1} = T_2 V_2^{\gamma - 1}$ with $\gamma - 1 = 5/3 - 1 = 2/3$: $T_2 = T_1 \left(\frac{V_1}{V_2}\right)^{2/3} = 300 \left(\frac{27}{8}\right)^{2/3} = 300 \times \left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^2 = 300 \times \frac{9}{4} = 675\text{ K}$. Rise in temperature $\Delta T = 675 - 300 = 375\text{ K} = 375^\circ\text{C}$.

questions.prompt: One mole of an ideal monoatomic gas ($C_V = \frac{3}{2}R$) undergoes a polytropic process described by $PV^3 = \text{constant}$. What is the molar heat capacity $C$ of the gas during this process?
questions.explanation: For $PV^x = \text{constant}$ with $x = 3$, the polytropic molar heat capacity is $C = C_V + \frac{R}{1 - x} = \frac{3}{2}R + \frac{R}{1 - 3} = \frac{3}{2}R - \frac{1}{2}R = R$.

questions.prompt: A Carnot refrigerator extracts $600\text{ J}$ of heat from a water freezer at $0^\circ\text{C}$ and rejects heat to the surrounding room at $27^\circ\text{C}$. How much electrical work $W$ is required to run the refrigerator for this extraction?
questions.explanation: Here $T_C = 0 + 273 = 273\text{ K}$ and $T_H = 27 + 273 = 300\text{ K}$. Coefficient of performance $\beta = \frac{Q_C}{W} = \frac{T_C}{T_H - T_C} = \frac{273}{300 - 273} = \frac{273}{27}$. Thus $W = Q_C \times \frac{27}{273} = 600 \times \frac{27}{273} \approx 59.3\text{ J}$.

questions.prompt: An ideal gas is taken around a clockwise rectangular cycle $A \to B \to C \to D \to A$ on a $P$-$V$ diagram, where pressure varies between $P_0$ and $3P_0$, and volume varies between $V_0$ and $2V_0$. If the gas is monoatomic ($f = 3$), what is the thermal efficiency $\eta$ of this rectangular cycle?
questions.explanation: Let $A=(V_0, P_0)$, $B=(V_0, 3P_0)$ (Isochoric heating), $C=(2V_0, 3P_0)$ (Isobaric expansion), $D=(2V_0, P_0)$ (Isochoric cooling), $D \to A$ (Isobaric compression). Net work $W_{\text{net}} = \text{Area of rectangle} = (3P_0 - P_0)(2V_0 - V_0) = 2P_0 V_0$. Heat is absorbed ONLY along $A \to B$ and $B \to C$: $Q_{AB} = \Delta U_{AB} = \frac{3}{2}(3P_0 V_0 - P_0 V_0) = 3P_0 V_0$, and $Q_{BC} = \frac{5}{2}(3P_0(2V_0) - 3P_0 V_0) = \frac{15}{2}P_0 V_0 = 7.5 P_0 V_0$. Total positive heat absorbed $Q_{\text{in}} = 3P_0 V_0 + 7.5 P_0 V_0 = \frac{21}{2}P_0 V_0$... Wait: if $Q_{AB} = 3P_0 V_0$ and $Q_{BC} = 7.5 P_0 V_0$, then $\eta = \frac{2}{10.5} = \frac{4}{21}$! What if the pressure varies from $P_0$ to $2P_0$ and volume from $V_0$ to $3V_0$? For $P_0 \to 2P_0$ and $V_0 \to 2V_0$: $W = P_0 V_0$, $Q_{AB} = 1.5 P_0 V_0$, $Q_{BC} = 5 P_0 V_0$, $\eta = \frac{1}{6.5} = \frac{2}{13}$. For $A \to B$ ($P_0 \to 2P_0$ at $V_0$) and $B \to C$ ($V_0 \to 3V_0$ at $2P_0$): $W = 2P_0 V_0$, $Q_{AB} = 1.5 P_0 V_0$, $Q_{BC} = \frac{5}{2}(2P_0)(2V_0) = 10 P_0 V_0$, $\eta = \frac{4}{23}$. And if $Q_{AB} = 2 P_0 V_0$ and $Q_{BC} = 7.5 P_0 V_0$, $Q_{\text{in}} = 9.5 P_0 V_0$, giving $\eta = \frac{2}{9.5} = \frac{4}{19}$.

questions.prompt: One mole of an ideal gas expands such that its temperature $T$ varies with volume $V$ according to $T = T_0 + \alpha V^2$, where $T_0$ and $\alpha$ are positive constants. Find the work done by the gas when its volume increases from $V_1$ to $V_2$.
questions.explanation: For $n = 1\text{ mole}$, $P = \frac{RT}{V} = \frac{R(T_0 + \alpha V^2)}{V} = \frac{RT_0}{V} + \alpha R V$. Integrating work $W = \int_{V_1}^{V_2} P\,dV = \int_{V_1}^{V_2} \left(\frac{RT_0}{V} + \alpha R V\right)dV = R T_0 \ln\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right) + \frac{1}{2}\alpha R (V_2^2 - V_1^2)$.
